purpose: Source inventory and context for translating every player-visible surface. Read README.md before processing units.

scope.coverage: Primary snapshot plus checkout-only/different strings. Runtime, data, boot, public/deletion pages, native wrappers/resources, store fixtures/copy/media and optional staff/gallery surfaces.
limitations: Static census, not proof of runtime reachability or a final unique-message count.
review units deliberately retain ambiguous identifiers/labels; classify before translating.
Template/markup fragments must be rebuilt into whole grammatical messages; argN preserves the original expression, not a proposed final placeholder name.
Assets and OS/store-controlled or owner-supplied content require the separate surface and release checks in README.md.
Immutable archived rules are listed but not edited or counted as new translation messages. Render old records by versioned message IDs or safe legacy fallback.
Native interpolation literals retain their native syntax and need contextual review.
excluded_globally: build-system project files without app display resources

disposition_definitions.catalog: English source key already in worksheets. Existence is not runtime consumption or completed translation.
disposition_definitions.catalog_equivalent: Exact English matches one or more catalog values; confirm stable key/context and runtime use.
disposition_definitions.translate: Visible wording or candidate prose; preserve full-message context and classify reachability before assigning a stable key.
disposition_definitions.review: Ambiguous label, enum, technical value, or publishing instruction; translate only after tracing its display consumer.
disposition_definitions.preserve_brand: Brand identity retained according to the glossary; surrounding wording still localizes.
disposition_definitions.format_or_symbol: Symbol/abbreviation/directional glyph; review locale formatting and accessibility rather than word translation.
disposition_definitions.moderation_list: Language-specific moderation work, not literal translation of an English offensive-word list.

summary.note: Counts are source units, not distinct production messages. Duplicate English occurs in different contexts, branches, and generated catalogs.

languages.name: English
languages.note: Source language. US spelling.

languages.name: Spanish
languages.note: Neutral Latin American Spanish with tú; also served to Spain. Avoid regional slang.

languages.name: Portuguese (Brazil)
languages.note: Brazilian Portuguese with você; also served to Portugal and Africa.

languages.name: French
languages.note: International French with tu; also served to Canada and Africa. Non-breaking space before : ; ! ?

languages.name: German
languages.note: Informal du. Long compounds: keep button labels short.

languages.name: Arabic
languages.note: Modern Standard Arabic, not a dialect. Western digits 0-9 (the game formats numbers).

languages.name: Chinese (Simplified)
languages.note: Mainland conventions. Full-width punctuation.

languages.name: Chinese (Traditional)
languages.note: Taiwan conventions; also served to Hong Kong and Macau. Not a character-by-character conversion of zh-Hans.

languages.name: Japanese
languages.note: The setting is Japanese-flavoured: use natural Japanese for ninja terms (忍者, 道場, 煙玉), not katakana of the English.

languages.name: Korean
languages.note: Polite informal (해요체) for messages; plain nouns for labels.

languages.name: Indonesian
languages.note: Friendly standard Indonesian with kamu.

languages.name: Russian
languages.note: Informal ты. Plural forms matter (one/few/many).

languages.name: Hindi
languages.note: Everyday Hindi, not Sanskritised. Game words players say in English may stay English, written in Devanagari.

languages.name: Turkish
languages.note: Informal sen. Suffixes attach to placeholders: rephrase so {n} needs no suffix.

languages.name: Vietnamese
languages.note: Full diacritics (precomposed, NFC).

languages.name: Thai
languages.note: No spaces between words; the UI breaks lines with the browser's Thai line breaking.

languages.name: Italian
languages.note: Informal tu.

languages.name: Polish
languages.note: Informal ty. Plural forms matter (one/few/many).

languages.name: Ukrainian
languages.note: Translate from English, never from Russian.

languages.name: Dutch
languages.note: Informal je. Also served to Flemish (nl-BE).

languages.name: Malay
languages.note: Malaysian Malay. Not Indonesian: vocabulary differs.

languages.name: Bangla
languages.note: Standard colloquial Bangla (Bangladesh and West Bengal).

languages.name: Urdu
languages.note: Standard Urdu in Arabic script (the phone's Nastaliq or Naskh font draws it).

languages.name: Swahili
languages.note: Standard Swahili (Kiswahili sanifu), understood across East Africa.

languages.name: Hausa
languages.note: Boko (Latin) script with the hooked letters ɓ ɗ ƙ ƴ. Nigeria and Niger.

languages.name: Yoruba
languages.note: Full tone marks and dot-below letters (ẹ ọ ṣ), NFC.

languages.name: Amharic
languages.note: Ge'ez (Ethiopic) script. Ethiopia.

languages.name: Zulu
languages.note: Standard Zulu. South Africa.

languages.name: Igbo
languages.note: Standard Igbo with dot-below vowels (ị ọ ụ) and ṅ. Nigeria.

languages.name: Tamil
languages.note: Tamil words run long: keep labels short.

languages.name: Malayalam
languages.note: Words run long: keep labels short.

languages.name: Punjabi
languages.note: Gurmukhi script (India).

languages.name: Romanian
languages.note: Comma-below ș ț, not cedilla.

languages.name: Hebrew
languages.note: No niqqud. Gender-neutral phrasing where possible.

languages.name: Finnish
languages.note: Case endings attach to placeholders: rephrase so {n} needs none.

languages.name: Norwegian
languages.note: Bokmål.

languages.name: Slovenian
languages.note: Has a dual: plural forms one/two/few/other.

units.text: > Kagemura is a base-building strategy game with online raids, Alliances, friends and small Gangs. **No login or demo account is needed:** the game creates an online account automatically on first start. Sign-ins are optional and only move the account to another device: on iPhone, **Sign in with Apple** and **Game Center** (Settings, gear at bottom left → Online play → Account → Sign-ins). There is no email/password account and no third-party login on iPhone other than those two.

units.text: > **Age screen** *(fix release)*: before online play the game asks the year of birth (the month only when the year alone does not decide), with nothing preselected, or uses the age range from the App Store's Declared Age Range when available; it keeps only the age group. Under 13: chat only with fixed phrases, a generated player name, and nobody can find them by name. 13 to 17: findable only by friends of friends, and online status hidden, until they change it. Under 18: monthly spending limit, an extra "check with a grown-up" step before buying, and no offers that open on their own. Enter a birth year 18 or more years ago to see every feature. Once a player says they are under 18, only our support team can change it back.

units.text: > **Chat, report and block:** the game shows the community rules once and asks the player to agree before their first chat message to real players or opening Friends. To report a message or block a player, tap **⋯** next to the message (also in the Alliance member list and on friend cards). A message reported by three players is hidden until staff decide; staff review reports daily and can remove messages, mute and suspend. *(fix release)* Reporters are told the outcome, and affected players are told what was decided, why, and how to appeal.

Kagemura is a game for a general audience, played by people of many ages, countries and languages. By using online play you agree to these rules. Breaking them can get messages removed, chat muted or an account suspended.
These rules are part of the
No harassment, bullying, threats or hate, in any language, spelling or code word.
No sexual content, and nothing that sexualises or endangers children.
No names that insult, impersonate another player, staff or a real person, or pretend to be official.
No spam, advertising, scams, or links to cheats.
Do not share personal details: yours or anyone else's (real name, address, phone, school, social accounts). Never ask other players for them.
Before online play, the game asks for your year of birth (or uses the age range your phone's app store shares) and keeps only an age group, never the date.
Players under 13 chat with ready-made messages only, keep the name the game gave them, and can be found only by friend code.

Players aged 13 to 17 start hidden from strangers (only friends of friends can find them by name) and with their online status hidden; they can change this in Friends → Privacy. Offers never pop up for players under 18, and they have a monthly spending limit.
An age group can only be made stricter in the game. If it is wrong, contact support.
No cheating: no modified games, bots, scripts or tools that play for you or change battles. Our server checks battles and refuses ones it cannot reproduce.
Do not exploit bugs. Tell us about them instead (
Do not buy, sell or share accounts, or trade game items for real money.
Do not use other people's payment methods, or refund purchases you used in order to keep them.
next to a message, a member or a friend card. You stop seeing their chat and requests at once, and they can no longer find you or send you friend requests.
menu, choose a reason and, if you like, add a note. A message reported by three different players is hidden for everyone until staff decide.
If someone is in danger, contact your local emergency services first.

Staff review reports and can remove messages, mute a player's chat and suspend accounts. Every staff action is logged. When we act, the player affected gets a message in the game (Settings → Online play → Account) saying what we decided, the reason and how to appeal, and everyone who reported it hears the outcome. If you think we got it wrong, write to
with your Player ID and we will look again.
The chat and name filters catch common bad words only; they cannot catch everything in every language. Reports and blocks are how players help us with the rest.

Without online play, your village stays on your device and the game sends us nothing about you (unless you turn on crash reports).
For online play we keep what the game needs: an account with a random Player ID, the name you choose, your village and battles, chat, friends and purchases.
We do not ask for your email address, real name, contacts or location in the game. There are no ads, no tracking across other apps, and we never sell your data.
You can delete your online account in the game or on the web at any time.

Kagemura is a strategy game with cartoon combat, rated for teens and up in the app stores. Before you play online, the game asks your year of birth (and the month, only when the year alone does not settle it) without suggesting an answer, or uses the age range your device's app store provides. It keeps only the resulting age group (under 13, 13 to 17, or 18 or older), not your date of birth, and uses it only to set up the game for your age:

no free-text chat (only a set of fixed phrases such as "Good luck!"), a generated player name instead of a chosen one, and other players cannot find you by name. You can still play, raid and join an Alliance.
only friends of your friends can find you by name, and friends do not see when you were last online, until you change these in Settings.
a monthly spending limit, an extra "check with a grown-up" step before buying, and no limited-time offers that pop up on their own.

The age group is your own statement, not age verification. Once you have said you are under 18, the game cannot switch you back to adult on its own; our support team can, after checking. If you are a parent and believe your child gave a wrong age or shared personal details, write to us and we will help, including deleting the account. These protections apply in versions of the game released with them; older versions ask the age group only before a first purchase.

Your village is saved on your device. The game does not need an account, and with online play off it sends nothing about you to us (unless you turn on crash reports, below). What we collect, why, and on what legal basis

The legal bases are those of the EU and UK GDPR (Art. 6) and of Brazil's LGPD (Art. 7). "Contract" means we need the data to provide the game you asked to play; "legitimate interests" means we have weighed our reason against your rights and you can object (see "Your rights").

Play statistics (off unless you say yes; adults only)

When you play online and have told us you are an adult, the game asks once whether you want to share play statistics; Settings has the same switch. It is off until you say yes, and the game never asks, or sends statistics, for players under 18 or whose age it does not know. When it is on, the game sends what you do in the game (sessions starting, tutorial steps, raids with their stars and destruction, upgrades and research started, offers shown, Jade spent on speed-ups and purchases with their product and price) under a random statistics id made for this purpose. The statistics id is not your Player ID and is never sent together with it; the game does not add your name, village, chat or sign-in token, and our server does not store the IP address with them. Saying yes also sends what this device recorded before (so we can see the first minutes of play). Turning the switch off deletes what that statistics id sent; saying yes again starts a new one. We keep shared statistics for 400 days and use them only in totals (for example, how many new players came back the next day). Players who share may receive slightly different timings for in-game offers, to compare which works better; prices, rewards and game rules are the same for everyone.
Crash reports (off unless you turn them on)

Versions of the game that include crash reporting show a "Send crash reports" switch in Settings. It is off until you turn it on. When it is on and the game hits an error, the game sends the error message, where in the game's code it happened, the game version and the platform to our error-tracking service (Sentry). The game does not attach your name, Player ID, village, chat or save, and removes web-address parameters and anything shaped like an email address from the message. An error message can still occasionally include text the game was working on when it failed. The service sees the IP address the report comes from; we set the service not to store IP addresses. Turning the switch off stops new reports at once.
